extracted.intended_audience: literary readers, poets, translators, and critics (aspiring writers and commentators)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging poetry, epic subjects, translation, diction, characterization, and didactic verse. Draws on examples (Milton, Wordsworth, Homer, Dryden, Pope, Virgil) to illustrate standards for poetic method, style, and translator qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic poem subject suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: "The destruction of Jerusalem is the only subject now remaining for an epic poem; a subject which, like Milton's Fall of Man, should interest all Christendom, as the Homeric War of Troy interested all Greece.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An epic subject should engage a whole civilization (e.g., all Christendom), assemble grandeur and splendour, allow for completion/fulfilment of prophecy or a mythic arc, present contrasted national/character types (here Roman and Jew), and exhibit awfulness, completeness, and justice. Difficulties in the subject must be mitigated or thrown into shade, as Milton did with Paradise Lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a mythology or quasi-mythology in epic
rubrics_metrics.description: "And yet there must be a mythology, or a quasi-mythology, for an epic poem.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An epic requires a system of mythic or quasi-mythic material to provide scope, symbolic depth, and a framework (completion of prophecies, cosmological or religious meaning) for grand national themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour-system (heptad) for poetic symbolism
rubrics_metrics.description: "Colours may best be expressed by a heptad, the largest possible formula for things finite... The heptad of things finite is in all cases reducible to the pentad.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using colour symbolically, consider a structured palette (a seven-part scheme with primary thesis/antithesis/prothesis and syntheses) rather than ad hoc colours; the text gives a specific schematic (Red as Prothesis, Yellow Thesis, Blue Antithesis; orange, indigo/violet as indifferences; green decomposable; a spurious/ artificial synthesis). This is a method for systematic colour symbolism in composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black as symbolic device
rubrics_metrics.description: "Black is the negation of colour in its greatest energy. Without lustre, it indicates or represents vacuity, as, for instance, in the dark mouth of a cavern; add lustre, and it will represent the highest degree of solidity, as in a polished ebony box.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use black differently depending on surface/lustre: matte black suggests vacuity, absence, emptiness; lustrous black suggests solidity, density, or highest material substance. Consider surface treatment when employing colour symbolism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translator qualifications for historical/theological works
rubrics_metrics.description: "The translator should be a man deeply imbued with his Bible, with the English writers from Henry the Seventh to Edward the Sixth, the Scotch divines of the 16th century, and with the old racy German.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For translating works like Luther's letters, choose someone steeped in the original religious texts, the historical English literary idiom of the target period, the contemporary divines, and the source-language idiom and tone—so the translation preserves theological nuance, historical register, and native flavour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of translatability by author/genre
rubrics_metrics.description: "If you take Sophocles, Catullus, Lucretius, the better parts of Cicero, and so on, you may, just with two or three exceptions ... translate page after page into good mother English, word by word, without altering the order; but you cannot do so with Virgil or Tibullus: if you attempt it, you will make nonsense.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different classical authors require different translation strategies: some idioms map almost directly to English and permit close, literal rendering; others (e.g., Virgil, Tibullus) demand reordering, paraphrase, and more adaptive translation to preserve sense and poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of iambic-sounding Christian names (metrical naming)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Never take an iambus as a Christian name. A trochee, or tribrach, will do very well. Edith and Rotha are my favourite names for women.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When naming characters, attend to metrical stress patterns: avoid names that impose an iambic foot if that is undesirable for prosody; prefer trochaic or tribrachic names to suit rhythm and euphony within verse or prose cadence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of adverbs and objectivity in epic style
rubrics_metrics.description: "The want of adverbs in the Iliad is very characteristic. With more adverbs there would have been some subjectivity, or subjectivity would have made them.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimizing adverbs contributes to an objective, impersonal epic tone. Excessive adverbial modification introduces subjectivity and may undermine the classical epic effect; consider restraint in adverb use to preserve impersonality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical writing: read for principles, not just facts
rubrics_metrics.description: "The only thing interesting to me was the principles to be evolved from, and illustrated by, the facts... After I had gotten my principles, I pretty generally left the facts to take care of themselves.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or evaluating history (and historical narrative), prioritize the extraction and exposition of general principles or patterns over mere chronicling of particulars; emphasize explanatory frameworks that make facts meaningful rather than cataloguing minutiae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of genius in characterization (progressive development)
rubrics_metrics.description: "You will find this a good gage or criterion of genius,--whether it progresses and evolves, or only spins upon itself. Take Dryden's Achitophel and Zimri ... every line adds to or modifies the character ... whereas, in Pope's Timon ... the first two or three couplets contain all the pith of the character.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate literary genius (especially in characterization) by whether a writer develops and evolves characters and ideas over the course of the work (progressive building) rather than presenting static, fully encapsulated types that merely repeat the initial premise. Progressive, accumulative characterization is a mark of depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue in verse and the poet's mode of address
rubrics_metrics.description: "Can dialogues in verse be defended? I cannot but think that a great philosophical poet ought always to teach the reader himself as from himself. A poem does not admit argumentation, though it does admit development of thought... I have no admiration for the practice of ventriloquizing through another man's mouth.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a rule, philosophical poetry should present development of thought originating in the poet's own voice rather than rely on didactic argumentation via dramatic dialogue or ventriloquism. Avoid making the poem a forum for direct argumentative debate; prefer subtle development and internal demonstration of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for a philosophic/pastoral epic (Wordsworthian plan)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The plan ... was, that Wordsworth should assume the station of a man in mental repose... treat man as man, --a subject of eye, ear, touch, and taste, in contact with external nature ... describe the pastoral and other states of society ... opening a melancholy picture of the present state ... thence he was to infer and reveal the proof of, and necessity for, the whole state of man and society being subject to, and illustrative of, a redemptive process in operation.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For composing a philosophic pastoral epic: adopt a contemplative narrator-position, ground philosophy in sensory experience and nature, chart social conditions from pastoral to urban, use melancholic diagnosis of degeneration, and culminate in an inferred redemptive or reconciliatory process that unifies anomalies—i.e., let thought grow organically from experience and social observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain contemplative stance for the philosophic poet
rubrics_metrics.description: "I think Wordsworth possessed more of the genius of a great philosophic poet ... but it seems to me that he ought never to have abandoned the contemplative position, which is peculiarly ... fitted for him.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A philosophic poet's strength often lies in a contemplative 'spectator ab extra' stance; abandoning that stance for other modes may weaken suitability and authority. Consider preserving an external contemplative perspective when the subject demands philosophy in poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Didactic poetry must be seasoned with personal interest
rubrics_metrics.description: "Mere didactics of practice, unless seasoned with the personal interests of the time or author, are inexpressibly dull to me.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Didactic verse should be enlivened by the author's personal voice, contemporary relevance, or particular interests; bare instruction or practice without personal inflection will likely be tedious to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of genius: metaphysical/ideal orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: "All genius is metaphysical; because the ultimate end of genius is ideal, however it may be actualized by incidental and accidental circumstances.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing 'genius' in creative work, consider its reach toward ideal or metaphysical concerns beyond mere technical execution or topicality. A work that aspires to or accomplishes an 'ideal' or metaphysical scope is more likely to be judged genuinely great.
